**My recommendation: make DisputePro a bank’s resolution workspace, with a connected customer experience and a live “follow this payment” view for judges.** The standout moment should be seeing a complaint become a verified change in the bank’s records, with the customer receiving the result.

I read the project Markdown files, Entire’s project context, recent commit history, and the current customer, console, and case-processing code. The key changes are `baaef64`—channels and supervisor—and `b392c74`—customer app and live desk. Those give us a stronger foundation than the interface currently communicates.

This is a proposal before implementation. The issues below come from source inspection; I haven’t run a browser walkthrough in this turn.

**What’s currently breaking the experience**

- **The customer starts by choosing a persona.** `/app` even marks people with problems. This conflicts with your documented “no customer pickers in the complaint flow” requirement and immediately makes the experience feel staged.
- **The bank starts inside an agent viewer.** The central question becomes “Which agent is running?” A bank operator needs “What needs my attention, why, and what can I safely do?”
- **“Autopilot” has two unrelated jobs:** generating synthetic complaints and enabling processing of recon cases. Turning off simulated traffic can therefore affect real queue behavior.
- **Failures disappear into the wrong category.** The case rail groups `FAILED` and `ESCALATED` under “Resolved.”
- **Customer conversations lose case context.** Complaints share one customer thread; a free-text follow-up can attach to the latest case awaiting information.
- **Some success claims are premature.** The UI hardcodes “penalty so far ₹0,” labels deadlines “met” whenever an outcome has a deadline, and the approval message can say a hold was requested without checking the corresponding action.

These need workflow corrections alongside the redesign.

**1. Give each audience a clear entrance**

| Surface | Purpose | Primary action |
|---|---|---|
| Landing page | Explain the problem and show verifiable value | **Explore the live bank** |
| Bank workspace | Prioritize exceptions and make decisions | **Review next case** |
| Customer app | Get help with a payment and track the answer | **Get help** |
| Judge walkthrough | Follow the same case across customer and bank views | **Follow this case** |

The walkthrough is a presentation layer over actual cases and events. It must not choose outcomes or invent activity.

For the customer app, open an already established sandbox session. Any account switching belongs in a clearly separated demo control, outside the customer journey.

**2. Customer flow: payment → help → certainty**

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Open payment] --> B[Get help]
    B --> C[Describe the issue]
    C --> D[Case receipt and tracking]
    D --> E{Enough information?}
    E -->|No| F[One focused question]
    F --> D
    E -->|Yes| G[Bank investigates]
    G --> H[Verified outcome and receipt]
    H --> I[View proof or ask for review]
```

The payment screen should show recipient, amount, date, status, and one obvious **Get help with this payment** action.

Offer plain-language issue shortcuts:

- Money deducted, recipient hasn’t received it.
- Merchant says the payment failed.
- I don’t recognise this payment.
- Something else.

Keep free text available. These shortcuts express the customer’s claim; evidence still determines the outcome.

After submission, show a **case receipt**, not just a chat bubble:

> **We’re checking your payment**  
> Your payment details are attached. You don’t need to submit another complaint.  
> Case reference · latest update · next expected update

Each case gets its own conversation and tracking page. If Intake needs clarification, show the question there, with relevant payment choices when available.

Customer-facing progress uses meaningful milestones:

**Received → Checking bank records → Action in progress → Outcome**

A fraud review can say “A specialist is reviewing this.” A partial hold must distinguish money secured from money refunded. A successful payment should end with proof of credit, not a generic green “resolved” badge.

**3. Bank flow: attention first, investigation second**

The bank lands on an **Attention** screen.

At the top, show a small operational summary derived from actual data:

- Cases requiring a decision.
- Cases approaching their applicable deadline.
- Cases blocked by unavailable evidence or failed actions.
- Cases completed today.

Below it, use a searchable queue:

| Priority | Case | Current finding | Deadline | Next action |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Approval needed | Customer / payment | Evidence supports proposed action | Time remaining | Review decision |
| Blocked | Customer / payment | Counterparty unavailable | Time remaining | Review recovery |
| Investigating | Customer / payment | Checking credit confirmation | Time remaining | Open case |

Every priority should explain itself. Avoid unexplained AI urgency scores.

Navigation stays small: **Attention · All cases · Activity**. Approvals and blocked cases are filters, not separate disconnected products.

Recon processing should operate independently of the sandbox traffic generator. Pausing synthetic arrivals must not stop the bank from clearing existing work.

**4. The signature screen: “Follow the money”**

This is where the product can become memorable.

Opening a case reveals a stable workspace:

```text
Case reference · Customer · Amount          Deadline / status

Payment path and observed state
Sending bank → NPCI → Receiving bank → Recipient
                          Evidence missing ↑

What we know                  Decision / next action
Evidence with sources         Proposed actions and amounts
Contradictions                Why approval is required
Latest verified update        Approve / decline / escalate

Timeline · Customer conversation · Technical trace
```

The payment path adapts to the case: merchant cases include the acquirer; inward exceptions show the bank’s suspense account.

**Each node represents an observed record.** Clicking it reveals the source, timestamp, reference, and relevant response. Missing evidence stays visibly unknown. A timeout appears at the affected party.

As investigation progresses, the same screen accumulates facts. It should not keep replacing its main content as different agents take control.

The agents remain visible through concise activity updates:

> “Receiving bank timed out. Checking available switch evidence.”

Detailed tool calls, model usage, and neatlogs traces belong in an expandable technical view.

**5. Approval becomes a precise decision**

Replace a generic “Approve and execute” card with a decision brief:

- **Finding:** what the evidence establishes.
- **Proposed actions:** each action and amount.
- **Reason for review:** the exact guardrail triggered.
- **Uncertainty:** what remains unconfirmed.
- **Customer update:** what will be communicated after execution.

Label the primary button with the actual action where possible. For multiple actions, use **Approve these actions**.

After approval, display execution separately:

**Approved → Executing → Confirmed / Partially completed / Failed**

An approval is not proof that money moved. Rejection should capture a reason and leave a clear next owner or next step.

**6. Make completion the strongest screen**

The existing before/after system comparison is one of the best ideas in the code. Promote it.

A completed case should produce a **resolution receipt** showing:

- The finding and supporting evidence.
- Confirmed monetary actions and references.
- Applicable deadline and actual completion time.
- Customer notification status.
- Human approval, when required.
- A link to the execution trace.

Keep the receipt available after a server restart. Today, the detailed live run depends on in-memory state.

Also preserve the distinction between **customer resolution** and **remaining bank recovery work**. A customer refund and an open chargeback can coexist.

**7. Visual direction: precise, calm, distinctive**

I’d use **deep navy navigation, warm off-white work surfaces, dark typography, and a restrained cobalt accent**.

- One primary sans-serif; monospace only for references and financial data.
- Comfortable 14–16px working text instead of the current abundance of tiny labels.
- Strong alignment, fine dividers, fewer nested cards.
- Compact status labels with text and icons; colour adds meaning.
- Amber for attention, red for failed or overdue states, green for confirmed success.
- Motion only when real evidence arrives or a state changes.
- Full-width mobile customer screens. Use a phone frame only in the judge walkthrough.
- On smaller bank screens, turn supporting panels into tabs while keeping decisions accessible.

The visual identity comes from the payment path, evidence presentation, and resolution receipt. Those should become recognisable DisputePro elements.

**8. The judge experience**

The strongest demonstration would be:

1. A judge writes a complaint in their own words.
2. The case appears in the bank queue.
3. **Follow this case** opens a connected customer/bank view.
4. The payment path fills with actual evidence.
5. The system either executes safely, requests clarification, or presents an approval.
6. Confirmed bank records change.
7. The customer receives the corresponding outcome.
8. The judge opens the receipt and its neatlogs trace.

Recon supplies a second compelling story: an exception discovered and addressed before the customer complains.

Keep sponsor evidence accessible from the walkthrough: neatlogs for execution traces, Entire for build history, and cfo.ai for the business plan once it exists. Preserve the pending label until then.

**I’d build the case workspace and resolution receipt first**, then the attention queue, customer journey, and finally the landing page and judge walkthrough. That gives the entire product one coherent story: **a payment problem arrives, the bank establishes what happened, takes a controlled action, and proves the result.**

The central experience should make five things obvious:

> **What triggered the agents → what they decided to investigate → which tools they used → why they changed direction → what they accomplished.**

Keep the customer and bank perspectives, but connect them through a visible agent team:

| Agent | What the visitor sees it actually doing |
|---|---|
| **Intake** | Understands the complaint, identifies the payment, asks a targeted question when needed |

| **Investigator** | Queries counterparties, compares evidence, exposes contradictions and unavailable sources |
| **Policy** | Applies the relevant rule and computes the deadline and amounts |
| **Resolver** | Proposes actions, requests approval when required, hands execution to the guarded executor |

**The orchestrator belongs at the centre of the screen.** Around it, agents become active as they receive real assignments. Selecting an agent reveals its assignment, tool calls, evidence, and concise decision explanation. The graph reflects actual routing—including skipped agents, retries, and escalation—rather than a fixed animation.

The main flow becomes:

1. **A real trigger arrives:** customer complaint or recon exception.
2. **The orchestrator opens a mission:** a plain-language objective tied to that payment.
3. **Agents investigate live:** findings and tool results appear alongside the team.
4. **A complication becomes visible:** conflicting evidence, unavailable bank, ambiguous complaint, or approval requirement.
5. **The orchestrator adapts:** the visitor sees the changed plan and its evidence.
6. **The executor confirms the result:** ledger change, customer response, and trace-backed receipt.

**Sponsors should have a visible, truthful role in that story:**

- **neatlogs — observe and improve the agents.** Open the actual case trace from the live investigation. Add a verified failure → fix → improved run comparison for judging.
- **Entire — explain how the agents were built and corrected.** Show linked checkpoints and relevant development history in a “Build evidence” view. It is currently development infrastructure, so we should present it accurately.
- **cfo.ai — demonstrate the business behind the product.** Complete the business plan using measured operational inputs from your MCP where supported. Show which inputs are measured and which are pricing assumptions.
- **Crustdata — only return with a meaningful investigative job.** We need a supported lookup that can affect an actual business or merchant investigation. Your docs currently establish no such role; putting its logo on a tool call would undermine the demo.

**The wow moment is the agent team encountering a problem, adapting visibly, and producing a verifiable banking outcome.** The polished customer flow and bank controls support that central experience. My earlier suggestion to tuck the agents into a technical drawer was the wrong emphasis for your goal.

**DisputePro is an agent-operated UPI resolution desk. A customer reports a payment problem—or the bank detects one—and an agent team investigates, decides what should happen, executes within guardrails, and returns proof.**

The product has three connected experiences: **customer help, the bank’s agent workspace, and a judge walkthrough that follows the same live case across both.** Below is the proposed end-to-end journey; some capabilities require changes to the current implementation.

**1. Enter the product**

The landing page leads with:

> **Payment stuck. Agents on it.**  
> Watch an AI team investigate across banking systems and resolve the exception with verifiable evidence.

Two entrances:

- **Open the agent desk** — enter Sahyadri Bank’s workspace.
- **Try customer help** — open an authenticated sandbox customer session.

A persistent **Sandbox · fictional bank** label establishes the environment. Account switching and traffic-generation controls live in a separate demo menu.

The landing page also provides sponsor evidence: actual neatlogs traces, Entire build history, and the cfo.ai plan when completed.

---

**2. Customer journey: “Where is my money?”**

The customer opens their payment history, selects a transaction, and taps **Get help**.

They can choose an issue or describe it freely:

> “Kal paise bheje the, mere account se kat gaye but usko mile nahi.”

There are two entry paths:

| Entry | What travels with the complaint |
|---|---|
| Help from a payment | Transaction reference, customer identity, message |
| General help chat | Customer identity and message; Intake identifies the payment |

**Intake visibly handles the ambiguity.**

If the transaction is clear, the customer receives a case receipt. If several payments match, Intake asks one focused question and presents the relevant options. It does not make the customer search for a UTR.

> **Which payment do you mean?**  
> Two payments match what you described.

Once identified, the case has a dedicated page containing:

- Payment and case reference.
- Current status.
- Conversation.
- Latest verified update.
- Any information the customer needs to provide.

The customer can leave and return. Their follow-up stays attached to this case.

Customer progress is simple:

**Received → Investigating → Taking action / Under review → Outcome**

The customer sees useful explanations, such as “We’re checking whether the receiving bank credited the payment.” They do not need to understand the agent architecture.

---

**3. The bank journey starts with the agent team**

The bank operator enters an **Agent desk** with three working areas:

```text
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Sahyadri Bank · Sandbox     Agent runtime     Connection status    │
├───────────────┬──────────────────────────────┬────────────────────┤
│ LIVE CASES    │ AGENT WORKSPACE              │ EVIDENCE & IMPACT  │
│               │                              │                    │
│ Needs review  │ Case objective               │ Payment path       │
│ Investigating │ Orchestrator's current plan  │ Verified facts     │
│ Blocked       │ Active agent team            │ Deadline           │
│ Queued        │ Decisions and tool activity  │ Proposed actions   │
│ Completed     │                              │ Confirmed changes  │
└───────────────┴──────────────────────────────┴────────────────────┘
```

The desk answers three questions immediately:

**What are the agents working on? What have they established? Where do they need me?**

Cases arrive through customer complaints or reconciliation. The supervisor starts eligible work within the configured capacity.

Queue priority reflects urgency and required intervention. Each case shows its deadline where applicable, current agent activity, and whether a human decision is needed.

Generating sandbox complaints is a separate control. Stopping that generator does not stop processing existing cases.

---

**4. Open a case: the orchestrator establishes the objective**

Selecting a case opens a stable workspace.

At the top:

> **Find where this payment stopped and determine the correct resolution.**

Below that, the **Orchestrator** displays its current plan and assignments, based on actual execution events.

For example:

> “The payment reference is identified. Investigator will compare the debit, switch status, and receiving-bank confirmation.”

The agent team sits prominently underneath:

**Intake · Orchestrator · Investigator · Policy · Resolver**

Each agent shows:

- Assigned task.
- Working, waiting, completed, or not required.
- Latest meaningful finding.
- Tools used and their results.
- A concise explanation of its decision.

The connections between agents reflect actual delegation. A case that needs only investigation should visibly finish without activating unnecessary agents.

**The user watches a team make progress, while the case remains the centre of attention.**

---

**5. Investigation: evidence builds in front of you**

The Investigator queries the relevant systems.

A payment-path visualization shows the records being checked:

**Sending bank → NPCI → Receiving bank → Recipient**

Merchant and inward-payment cases show their relevant participants.

As responses arrive, the workspace adds evidence:

- Debit confirmed.
- Switch status retrieved.
- Receiving-bank response received.
- Reversal found—or not found.
- Merchant confirmation checked, where relevant.

Every finding opens its underlying source, timestamp, and reference. Unknown information remains marked **Unknown**.

Alongside this, the agent activity explains consequential choices:

> “The receiving bank is unavailable. Retrying the request.”

If the retry fails, show the next actual decision: use other sufficient evidence, wait, or escalate. Never animate a successful connection that did not happen.

**This is the first major judge moment: the system encounters uncertainty and responds visibly.**

---

**6. The workflow branches according to evidence**

The product must make different outcomes feel intentional.

| Finding | Agent journey | Customer outcome |
|---|---|---|
| Payment already reversed | Investigator → Orchestrator closes with proof | See the reversal reference |
| Recipient credited | Investigator → Orchestrator closes with proof | See credit confirmation |
| Unresolved payment failure | Investigator → Policy → Resolver | Corrective action and receipt |
| Inward funds stuck in suspense | Investigator → Policy → Resolver | Verified return or applicable resolution |
| Suspected fraud | Investigator → Policy → Resolver → Human review | Review status, then confirmed actions |
| Evidence insufficient | Clarification, waiting, or escalation | Clear next step; no false success |

A shorter route is itself evidence of agency: **the orchestrator knows when more work is unnecessary.**

---

**7. Policy and Resolver turn findings into a decision**

When needed, Policy presents a readable ruling:

- Classification supported by the evidence.
- Applicable rule and source.
- Deadline.
- Amount owed, including compensation where applicable.
- Any uncertainty requiring review.

Resolver then creates an action plan.

Each action is explicitly **Proposed**, with its amount, target system, and reason. Proposed actions must look different from completed actions.

The guarded executor validates the plan, recomputes monetary amounts, checks for prior execution, and determines whether approval is required.

Two paths follow:

**Within automatic authority:** execute and verify.

**Human approval required:** pause the relevant actions and bring the case to the operator’s attention.

---

**8. Human journey: review a decision, then supervise execution**

The operator receives a focused decision brief:

> **Your approval is required**  
> Here is what the agents established, what they propose, and why this requires review.

The screen contains:

- Evidence supporting the decision.
- Exact proposed actions and amounts.
- Guardrail that triggered approval.
- Missing or uncertain evidence.
- Expected customer communication.

Actions:

**Approve these actions · Decline with reason · Escalate**

Approval moves the case to **Executing**, not **Resolved**.

Each action then receives its own result:

**Confirmed · Failed · Awaiting confirmation**

If only some actions succeed, the case shows partial completion and the remaining work. A retry rechecks existing effects to prevent duplicate financial actions.

The operator’s decision and subsequent results become part of the case history.

---

**9. Completion: both sides receive proof**

The customer receives an outcome in the case’s channel and language, supported by confirmed results.

Examples of outcome types:

- Refund confirmed, with amount and reference.
- Payment credited, with evidence.
- Previous reversal located.
- Funds partially secured; remaining investigation continues.
- Specialist review required, with an honest next step.

The bank sees a **resolution receipt**:

| Receipt section | Contents |
|---|---|
| Finding | What happened and how it was established |
| Agent decisions | Which agents acted and why |
| Execution | Confirmed actions, amounts, references |
| Timing | Applicable deadline and actual completion time |
| Human oversight | Approval or escalation record |
| Customer communication | Message and recorded delivery status |
| Observability | Link to the actual neatlogs trace |

Customer resolution and bank recovery remain distinct. A refund can be completed while a chargeback remains open.

The receipt persists across refreshes and server restarts.

---

**10. Sponsor journey: inspect the execution, improvement, and business**

Sponsors have clear roles connected to the product.

| Sponsor | Where it appears | What the visitor can verify |
|---|---|---|
| **neatlogs** | Case activity → **Open trace**; agent-quality view | Actual agent/tool execution, failures, timing, and measured before/after improvements |
| **Entire** | **How we built and improved this** | Checkpoints, change history, and evidence behind fixes |
| **cfo.ai** | **Business viability** | Business plan informed by measured operational inputs where supported, with assumptions labelled |
| **Crustdata** | Conditional investigative integration | A supported business lookup that materially changes a decision |

**Crustdata is currently removed in your repository.** Its return needs a concrete supported investigative use case. cfo.ai is also pending. These should not appear as live integrations until implemented and verified.

Entire supports development provenance; neatlogs supports runtime observability. Making those distinct gives the sponsor story credibility.

---

**11. Judge journey: follow one real case across the product**

The walkthrough connects everything without switching between unrelated demos:

1. **Write a complaint** in the customer experience.
2. **Follow this case** into the bank’s agent workspace.
3. Watch Intake identify the payment.
4. Watch the Orchestrator delegate.
5. Inspect tool results and evidence as they arrive.
6. Observe the actual branch: direct closure, corrective action, clarification, or approval.
7. See confirmed changes in the sandbox bank.
8. Return to the customer’s outcome.
9. Open the neatlogs trace and linked build evidence.
10. Inspect the business plan and its assumptions.

A second journey starts with reconciliation and demonstrates the proactive promise: **the bank finds an exception before a customer has to complain.**

During longer runs, keep meaningful evidence and current activity visible. Show elapsed time and connection state; never invent percentage progress.

**The main dashboard**

The map occupies the most space. The panels support it.

**1. Show the complaint entering the system**

At the top of the map, show the actual origin:

**UPI complaint · Help chat · Reconciliation**

Clicking it reveals the original message and attached payment details. This keeps the human problem visible throughout the investigation.

The next node is **Intake**.

- If the complaint includes a valid payment reference, show **Payment identified**.
- If Intake finds the transaction from the message, show the match and supporting details.
- If it cannot distinguish between transactions, branch to **Waiting for customer**.

That waiting branch contains the actual question. When the customer answers, a new event reconnects the case to Intake. The previous question remains in the history.

The map never pretends the case is still investigating while it is waiting.

**2. Make the orchestrator’s routing the centrepiece**

Here is the conceptual map. The live UI expands only the relevant branches:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    C[Complaint or recon exception] --> I[Intake]
    I -->|Payment identified| O[Orchestrator]
    I -->|Needs clarification| Q[Ask customer]
    Q -->|Customer replies| I

    O --> V[Investigator]
    V --> D{Orchestrator reviews evidence}

    D -->|Already reversed or credit confirmed| P[Close with proof]
    D -->|Corrective action needed| R[Policy]
    D -->|Insufficient evidence| W[Wait or escalate]

    R --> S[Resolver proposes actions]
    S --> G{Executor checks guardrails}

    G -->|Within automatic authority| E[Execute]
    G -->|Approval required| H[Human review]

    H -->|Approved| E
    H -->|Declined| X[Record reason and next step]

    E --> K{Verify action results}
    K -->|Confirmed| F[Outcome and customer update]
    K -->|Partial or failed| B[Recovery or escalation]
    P --> F
```

**The orchestrator node explains each consequential branch.**

For example:

> **Decision: close with proof**  
> Receiving-bank evidence confirms the recipient was credited. No corrective financial action is proposed.

Or:

> **Decision: request policy assessment**  
> The evidence indicates an unresolved payment failure.

These are concise, recorded decision explanations linked to evidence—not a stream of raw model reasoning.

**3. Agent cards show work, not just activity**

Each node is a compact card:

```text
INVESTIGATOR                              Working
Verify whether the recipient was credited

✓ Core banking: debit found
✓ NPCI: status retrieved
↻ Receiving bank: retrying after timeout

3 tool calls                         View evidence →
```

The card answers:

- What is this agent responsible for?
- What is it doing now?
- What has it established?
- What is blocking it?

Clicking **Investigator** opens its assignment and findings in the right panel. Clicking **Receiving bank** opens that specific tool call, response status, timestamp, and relevant data.

Raw payloads are one further expansion away.

**4. Draw the actual path as it unfolds**

Before execution, show only the known entry and the next pending step. As events arrive:

- The assigned agent becomes active.
- A tool result adds a finding.
- A recorded routing decision draws a labelled connection.
- A completed node remains available for inspection.
- An unused agent is labelled **Not required** in the team summary.

For a confirmed-credit complaint, the visible journey becomes:

**Complaint → Intake → Orchestrator → Investigator → Proof → Customer update**

For a refund requiring approval:

**Complaint → Intake → Investigation → Policy → Resolver → Approval → Execution → Verification**

This makes the intelligence visible: different evidence produces different routes.

Use a stable layout. New events should not repeatedly rearrange the graph or move the node someone is reading. Include **Follow live** and **Fit workflow** controls; manual inspection pauses automatic following.

**5. Approval changes the screen’s emphasis**

When approval is required, the human-review node turns amber and the case moves into **Needs approval**.

The right panel becomes a decision workspace:

```text
YOUR DECISION IS REQUIRED

Why
[Exact guardrail that triggered review]

Evidence
[Verified findings with source links]

Proposed actions
[Action]   [Amount]   [Target system]
[Action]   [Amount]   [Target system]

Uncertainty
[Anything still unconfirmed]

[Approve these actions]
[Decline with reason]    [Escalate]
```

After approval, the approval node records the reviewer and time. The execution node activates. **The green completion state appears only after the relevant action results are confirmed.**

If the operator declines, the map shows the recorded reason and next step. It does not display a successful ending.

**6. Give failure and waiting their own visual language**

| State | On the map | Available interaction |
|---|---|---|
| Working | Blue active node, current task | Inspect live activity |
| Waiting for customer | Amber question node | Read the question and conversation |
| Waiting for approval | Amber human-review node | Review and decide |
| Counterparty unavailable | Warning on the affected tool | Inspect retries and next decision |
| Partially completed | Individual action results | Inspect completed and outstanding work |
| Execution failed | Red action node | Review safe recovery options |
| Completed | Green verified outcome | Open receipt and proof |

A network disconnect gets a separate **Live connection lost** banner with the last-update time. It must not be confused with an agent failure.

**7. Make the outcome a visible transformation**

When the case finishes, the graph remains on screen, with its completed path intact.

A result card appears at its end:

> **Outcome confirmed**  
> What happened · what changed · customer update status

```text
BANK RECORD              BEFORE              AFTER
Relevant balance         Recorded value      Verified value
Reversal status          Recorded state      Confirmed state
Complaint record         Previous state      New reference
```

Only show changes that were actually observed.

The customer’s final message appears beside that result, connecting the technical work to the original complaint.

**8. Add interaction that helps users understand the agents**

I’d include these six interactions:

- **Click an agent:** inspect its assignment, tools, findings, and decision.
- **Click a connection:** see why that route was chosen.
- **Click a finding:** open its supporting evidence.
- **Click an action:** trace it back to policy and evidence.
- **Follow live:** keep the current activity in view without losing the selected case.
- **Replay timeline:** inspect recorded events from a completed run, clearly labelled as replay.

Use a light, spacious canvas with a dark navigation shell. Agent cards share one consistent structure; state colours carry operational meaning. Connections are restrained, labelled, and animated only when real events occur.

At normal zoom, users see the journey. Selecting a node reveals detail. On smaller screens, present the same graph as a vertical sequence with expandable branches and a full-screen detail drawer.

**The central design rule: every visible movement must correspond to an actual event, every branch must have an understandable reason, and every completed action must have proof.** That gives you an agent-first dashboard that is both impressive to watch and useful to operate.

# DisputePro product review and iteration plan

Reviewed 2026-10-10 against commits `21340b6`, `bef84cc`, and `c673d20`, current source, and the local product on port 3001.

## Assessment

The agent/executor foundation is worth keeping. The current presentation does not yet make a convincing top-five case:
viewers must navigate too much, live work can happen before they reach it, and the customer receipt can contradict the
execution record. Ranking cannot be predicted without seeing competing submissions.

The intended demonstration is one coherent case: complaint → evidence → routing decision → proposed action → approval
when required → verified bank record → a clear reply to the same customer. A good live run should make each transition
understandable without the presenter explaining which button to find.

## Findings, in priority order

| Priority | Observed problem | Fix and acceptance criterion |
|---|---|---|
| P0 | cfo.ai remains a placeholder. The official event requires its business plan. | Author pricing, costs, revenue and runway in cfo.ai; include a shareable artifact. Our MCP endpoint alone is not proof of using cfo.ai. |
| P0 | Send posts the complaint before offering Watch agents (`app/app/page.tsx`). | Submit only after the bank workspace opens. Cancel must retain the message and create no case. Refresh must not silently resubmit. Iteration 1 addresses this. |
| P0 | The tour covers controls on mobile, changes panels, and waits on particular agents. | Replace the eight-step overlay with optional in-flow guidance derived from case state. No blocked Next button, no automatic welcome popup, no forced agent selection. Iteration 1 addresses this. |
| P0 | Recorded case DP-2620 shows a confirmed refund, but the customer reply says actions were submitted and approval might be needed. `_outcome` prefers the Resolver's pre-execution message. | Produce the customer receipt from confirmed execution state; separately describe completed, proposed, failed and scheduled actions. Verify automatic resolution, approval and partial-failure replies. |
| P0 | Six recon cases were queued with no working cases in the inspected desk. `supervisor.loop` gates RECON on synthetic-arrival autopilot; the UI says arrivals are independent and provides no per-case start action. | Make processing policy explicit and consistent. Preferred: recon processes whenever capacity is available, independent of generated arrivals. Test with arrivals off. |
| P1 | The demo opens Aarav's routine payments; story presets can point to transactions already resolved by previous demos. | Give guided visitors a clear scenario entry and disclose existing outcomes. Introduce an isolated, resettable demo session before promising a fresh run. Never reset shared cases behind another viewer. |
| P1 | The workflow map lists roles and call counts but makes the crucial decision hard to spot. | Above the graph, surface the latest evidence and the next action with its reason and source. Keep raw tool responses expandable. The viewer should explain why the route changed after reading one sentence. |
| P1 | Resolution proof competes with a large map and a long narrow report. Mobile puts inspection below the workflow. | Prioritize the decision panel during approval and the verified receipt at completion. Use explicit Workflow / Evidence / Outcome views on narrow screens; keep the case context visible. |
| P1 | Long-running model sessions lack an overall wall-clock timeout in `agent_codex.py`. | Bound agent duration, show last activity and recovery status, and release capacity on timeout. Preserve confirmed actions; never blindly retry a financial write. Test a stalled subprocess. |
| P1 | Stream effects reset on status changes, and follow mode can move readers away from evidence they are inspecting. | Keep one stable stream per run, reconnect after a real resume, and make inspection versus following explicit. Check completion, approval, reconnect and replay. |
| P1 | The landing hero animates a fixed historical run with a working indicator; generic copy promises every payment resolves before the deadline. | Label the animation as an illustrated recorded run and scope claims to demonstrated outcomes. Iteration 1 corrects the most visible claims. |

| **Repeated demos lose their impact** | Stories reuse already-resolved payments. Give each demo an isolated, fresh case without resetting other viewers’ work. |
| **The graph shows activity better than judgment** | Surface three things prominently: **what was found → why the route changed → what happens next**. Keep raw calls expandable. |
| **Approval and resolution feel cramped** | Give the proposed actions and final receipt more space when those stages become relevant. |
| **Long model waits lack clear recovery** | Add bounded timeouts, last-activity status, and explicit recovery while preserving confirmed actions. |
| **Sponsor evidence is incomplete** | Finish the cfo.ai plan and show one measurable improvement through linked neatlogs traces and an Entire checkpoint. |
| **Economics need correction** | Zero marginal model billing excludes subscription, hosting, support, and reviewer costs. Model those explicitly. |

"""Company research for DisputePro's go-to-market plan, never a fraud signal."""
import re
from datetime import datetime, timezone

import httpx
import config

ENDPOINT = "https://api.crustdata.com/company/identify"


async def identify_companies(domains: list[str], *, transport=None) -> dict:
    cleaned = list(dict.fromkeys(d.strip().lower() for d in domains))
    if not cleaned or len(cleaned) > 10 or any(not re.fullmatch(r"(?=.{3,253}$)(?:[a-z0-9](?:[a-z0-9-]*[a-z0-9])?\.)+[a-z]{2,63}", d) for d in cleaned):
        raise ValueError("Provide 1–10 company website domains, not URLs, emails or UPI addresses")
    if not config.CRUSTDATA_API_KEY:
        raise RuntimeError("Crustdata API key is not configured")
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=25, transport=transport) as client:
        response = await client.post(ENDPOINT, headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {config.CRUSTDATA_API_KEY}",
                                      "x-api-version": "2025-11-01"}, json={"domains": cleaned, "exact_match": True})
    if response.status_code != 200:
        raise RuntimeError(f"Crustdata lookup failed (HTTP {response.status_code}); no company conclusion was made")
    raw = response.json()
    if not isinstance(raw, list):
        raise RuntimeError("Unexpected Crustdata response; no company conclusion was made")
    entries = []
    for domain in cleaned:
        entry = next((e for e in raw if e.get("matched_on", "").lower() == domain), {})
        matches = []
        for match in entry.get("matches", []):
            company = match.get("company_data", {})
            info = company.get("basic_info", {})
            matches.append({"company_id": company.get("crustdata_company_id") or info.get("crustdata_company_id"),
                            "confidence_score": match.get("confidence_score"),
                            **{k: info.get(k) for k in ("name", "primary_domain", "website", "employee_count_range", "industries")}})
        entries.append({"domain": domain, "status": "matched" if matches else "no_match", "candidates": matches})
    return {"provider": "Crustdata", "endpoint": ENDPOINT, "captured_at": datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(),
            "purpose": "Target-bank research for business planning; not customer or merchant risk scoring",
            "limitations": ["Company matches are not customers, sales leads or evidence of buying intent.",
                            "No match is inconclusive and must never be treated as fraud.",
                            "Company size does not establish dispute volume or willingness to pay."],
            "companies": entries}

import asyncio
import json
import logging
import time

import config

from engine.run import Run
from engine.bank_workflow import orchestrate_bank
from engine.orchestrator import decide
from . import bank_seed, store, supervisor

def cases():

    rows = [store._enrich(r) for r in db.q("SELECT * FROM desk_cases WHERE id LIKE 'BK-%'")]
    return sorted(rows, key=lambda c: (c['created_at'][:10] != today, c['created_at'], c['id']))


def persist(run):
    payload = {k: getattr(run, k) for k in ('case', 'brain', 'facts', 'pending_plan', 'usage', 'calls', 'trace_url', 'status', '_seq')}
    payload['elapsed_ms'] = run.ms()
    db.ex('INSERT OR REPLACE INTO bank_run_state VALUES (?,?)', run.id, json.dumps(payload, default=str))


def restore(run_id):
    if run_id in supervisor.RUNS:
        return supervisor.RUNS[run_id]
    saved = db.q1('SELECT payload FROM bank_run_state WHERE run_id=?', run_id)
    if not saved:
        raise HTTPException(409, 'Approval checkpoint is unavailable. Manual reconciliation is required.')
    data = json.loads(saved['payload'])
    run = Run(data['case'], data['brain'], 0)
    run.id = run_id
    for key, val in data.items():
        if key != 'elapsed_ms': setattr(run, key, val)
    run.t0 = time.monotonic() - data['elapsed_ms']/1000
    run.history = [json.loads(r['event']) for r in db.q('SELECT event FROM desk_events WHERE run_id=? ORDER BY seq', run_id)]
    run.closed = True
    supervisor.RUNS[run_id] = run
    return run


def new_run(c, brain=None):
    case = {**supervisor._run_case(c), 'bank_ledger': True}
    run = Run(case, brain or config.brain(), 0)
    supervisor.RUNS[run.id] = run
    store.update_case(c['id'], status='WORKING', run_id=run.id)
    return run


async def drive(run, work):
    try:
        # A slow/downstream call cannot strand the ledger indefinitely. Never retry
        # potentially partial financial work automatically after this boundary.
        await asyncio.wait_for(work, timeout=180)
        supervisor._apply(run, run.case['id'], run.facts['outcome'])
    except (Exception, asyncio.CancelledError) as exc:
        reason = ('Run exceeded its processing limit; reconcile recorded actions before continuing.'
                  if isinstance(exc, TimeoutError) else str(exc) or 'Run interrupted; reconciliation required.')
        log.warning('Bank case %s interrupted: %s', run.case['id'], reason)
        actions = run.facts.get('validation', {}).get('approved', [])
        outcome = {'status': 'ESCALATED', 'headline': 'Investigation required', 'summary': reason,
                   'case_type': run.facts.get('findings', {}).get('case_type', 'UNKNOWN'),
                   'findings': run.facts.get('findings', {'summary': reason, 'evidence': []}),
                   'actions': actions, 'rejected': [], 'ruling': run.facts.get('ruling'),
                   'governance': run.facts.get('governance'), 'chain': run.facts.get('chain'),
                   'trace_url': run.trace_url, 'usage': run.usage,
                   'ops': {'seconds': round(run.ms()/1000, 1), 'api_calls': len(run.calls), 'human_touches': 0}}
        run.status = 'ESCALATED'
        run.facts['outcome'] = outcome
        store.update_case(run.case['id'], status='ESCALATED', headline=outcome['headline'], outcome=outcome)
        await run.emit('run_failed', error=reason, outcome=outcome)
        if isinstance(exc, asyncio.CancelledError): raise
    finally:
        persist(run)
        run.close()


async def ensure_seed():
    global _initialized
    if _initialized: return
    async with _init_lock:
        if _initialized: return
        bank_seed.seed()
        # These are explicitly labelled pre-reviewed fixtures. They perform real
        # sandbox reads and validation but never execute the held payment plans.
        for cid in ('BK-021', 'BK-022'):
            c = store.get_case(cid)
            if c['status'] == 'QUEUED':
                run = new_run(c, 'rules')
                run.case['pre_reviewed_fixture'] = True
                await drive(run, orchestrate_bank(run))
        _initialized = True


@router.get('/ledger')
async def ledger_view():
    await ensure_seed()
    rows = cases()
    counts = {'all': len(rows), 'queued': 0, 'approval': 0, 'investigate': 0, 'completed': 0}
    for c in rows:
        group = {'QUEUED': 'queued', 'NEEDS_YOU': 'approval', 'RESOLVED': 'completed',
                 'ESCALATED': 'investigate', 'FAILED': 'investigate', 'NEEDS_INFO': 'investigate'}.get(c['status'])
        if group: counts[group] += 1
    return {'cases': rows, 'counts': counts, 'queue': STATE, 'model': config.model_name(),
            'brain': config.brain(), 'bank': db.OUR_BANK, 'target_seconds': 60, 'target_range': [60,90]}


class QueueRequest(BaseModel):
    on: bool


@router.post('/queue')
async def queue(req: QueueRequest):
    await ensure_seed()
    STATE['enabled'] = req.on
    return dict(STATE)


class DecisionRequest(BaseModel):
    approve: bool
    reviewer: str = Field(min_length=2, max_length=80)
    reason: str = Field(default='', max_length=500)


@router.post('/cases/{cid}/decision')
async def decision(cid: str, req: DecisionRequest):
    await ensure_seed()
    c = store.get_case(cid) if cid.startswith('BK-') else None
    if not c: raise HTTPException(404, 'Bank ledger case not found')
    if c['status'] != 'NEEDS_YOU': raise HTTPException(409, 'This case is not awaiting approval')
    if not req.approve and not req.reason.strip(): raise HTTPException(422, 'Add a reason for investigation')
    if _work_lock.locked(): raise HTTPException(409, 'Pause the queue and wait for the active case before reviewing this payment')
    async with _work_lock:
        # Recheck after acquiring serialization lock.
        if store.get_case(cid)['status'] != 'NEEDS_YOU': raise HTTPException(409, 'Decision already recorded')
        run = restore(c['run_id'])
        if not run.pending_plan: raise HTTPException(409, 'No held plan to approve')
        run.facts['review_reason'] = req.reason.strip()
        run.closed = False
        store.update_case(cid, status='WORKING')
        STATE.update(active_case_id=cid, started_at=db.iso(db.now()))
        try:
            await drive(run, decide(run, req.approve, req.reviewer.strip()))
        finally:
            STATE.update(active_case_id=None, started_at=None)
    return store.get_case(cid)


async def loop():
    while True:
        if STATE['enabled'] and not _work_lock.locked():
            try:
                await ensure_seed()
                async with _work_lock:
                    c = next((c for c in cases() if c['status']=='QUEUED'), None)
                    if not c:
                        STATE['enabled'] = False
                    else:
                        STATE.update(active_case_id=c['id'], started_at=db.iso(db.now()))
                        run = new_run(c)
                        try:
                            await drive(run, orchestrate_bank(run))
                        finally:
                            STATE.update(active_case_id=None, started_at=None)
            except asyncio.CancelledError:
                raise
            except Exception:
                log.exception('Bank queue tick failed')
                STATE['enabled'] = False
            # Brief receipt dwell, independent of actual run timing.
            await asyncio.sleep(3)
        else:
            await asyncio.sleep(.4)

I found the latest changes: the desk now runs **three cases per click**, has no Follow live toggle, uses independently scrolling columns, and the docs report **23 tests**.

One EC2 instance is enough for this demo. The deployment script needs updating first: it currently exposes HTTP ports directly, and the new queue, approval and reset endpoints need protection before the site goes public. The video should show the current three-case flow and clearly label any sped-up footage.

**Use one EC2 server for both frontend and backend.** They run as separate processes on the same machine. That fits the current architecture and the $25 budget.

I read the updated README, CLAUDE.md, bank-console contract, hackathon log and deployment script, plus commit `8c7555b`. The video plan below reflects the latest **three-case batches, updated layout and retired customer portal**.

**The hosting setup I recommend**

```text
Public HTTPS URL
       │
     Caddy
       ├── Website → Next.js frontend :3000
       └── /api/*  → FastAPI backend :8000
                          ├── Codex agents
                          ├── Local sandbox adapters
                          ├── SQLite records
                          └── neatlogs traces
```

| Component | Decision |
|---|---|
| Server | One `t3.small`, us-east-1, inside `Hackathon_VPC` |
| OS | Ubuntu 24.04; explicitly install the tested Python version |
| Storage | 20 GB gp3; persistent databases outside deployment folders |
| Frontend | Production Next.js build |
| Backend | FastAPI, **one worker**, one transaction processing at a time |
| Process management | Two systemd services; automatic restart |
| HTTPS | Caddy in front of both services |
| Address | A subdomain of `prabhatgp.me` if you control its DNS; otherwise the documented sslip.io route |

A single backend worker matters: the queue and live run registry currently live partly in process memory. Starting multiple workers would require additional coordination.

The server runs the application and agent tools; the model itself runs remotely. A GPU is unnecessary. Two GB RAM should be workable for this limited demo, with swap for build-time headroom and a memory check during the first deployed batch.

**Expected AWS cost**

| Item | Approximate monthly cost |
|---|---:|
| t3.small, continuously running | $15.26 |
| One public IPv4 address | $3.65 |
| 20 GB gp3 storage | $1.60 |
| **Estimated base total** | **$20.51/month** |

That is roughly **$4.75 for seven days**, before extras. These estimates use AWS’s published compute, IPv4 and storage rates; credit eligibility and remaining balance still need checking in your account. [EC2 pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/ec2/instance-types/t3/), [IPv4 pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/vpc/pricing/), [EBS pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/ebs/pricing/).

For this budget, use EC2 without a load balancer, NAT gateway or separate database service. Configure CPU-credit behaviour deliberately: T3 Unlimited can incur additional charges. Set spend alerts and a shutdown date after judging.

**The deployment sequence**

1. **Prepare the current release.** Deploy the reviewed commit; keep the existing rule that merging `qa` into `main` needs your instruction.
2. **Update the deployment script.** It currently builds against `http://PUBLIC_IP:8000` and exposes both applications directly. Change this to one HTTPS origin with Caddy routing.
3. **Protect the public demo.** The new bank queue, approval and reset routes currently lack authentication. Keep the homepage public, give judges controlled desk access, restrict reset to the operator, and limit paid/model-triggering actions. Three cases per click alone does not prevent repeated clicks.
4. **Keep internal services private.** Bind application ports to localhost. Expose HTTPS publicly; restrict SSH. Sandbox and per-agent MCP endpoints remain internal. Expose the separate business MCP endpoint only if needed, with its existing bearer protection.
5. **Configure the runtime.** Install Node, Python, Codex and dependencies. Authenticate Codex under the same OS user that runs the backend. Store secrets server-side.
6. **Apply your deployment-model instruction.** The docs specify `gpt-6.1-sol`, medium effort. Verify access and measure it on EC2 before making performance claims—the recorded Luna timings do not establish this model’s speed.
7. **Verify the deployed journey.** HTTPS, live event streaming, a three-case batch, approval, investigation, persisted receipts and recovery after restart. Confirm the model is actually running rather than falling back to rules.
8. **Record the video, then leave the demo ready for judges.** Save genuine footage and receipts before resetting anything.

This is a suitable **hackathon deployment**, with a single-machine failure point. Two servers would add expense without fixing the current shared-state limitations.

**For the video, choose 75 seconds.** Spend most of it showing agents doing work, not scrolling through the homepage. Use one automatic resolution and a short cut to an approval case.

Copy this prompt into Claude:

---

Create a polished **75-second product demonstration video for DisputePro**, built at neatHack.

Use the current repository and deployed product as the source of truth. Read `README.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `docs/bank-console.md` and `hackathon.md` before recording.

Deliver a 16:9 MP4, ideally 3840×2160, with clear English voiceover, readable captions, restrained transitions and quiet background music. Use actual interface recordings and genuine sponsor evidence. Keep cursor movement deliberate and zoom into the relevant panel rather than showing tiny full-screen text.

The product is **one bank’s failed-UPI operations desk**. It has one master agent, three specialists, mandatory RBI governance and a deterministic execution engine. There is no customer portal.

Follow this storyboard:

| Time | Screen and action | Exact voiceover |
|---|---|---|
| **0–3s** | Tight crop of a failed transaction; introduce DisputePro’s logo. Overlay: “Failed payment. Growing backlog.” | “Failed UPI payments shouldn’t become tomorrow’s backlog.” |
| **3–8s** | Reveal the bank desk: ledger on the left, agent workspace on the right. | “DisputePro gives bank operations teams an AI-powered recovery desk.” |
| **8–14s** | Brief deadline graphic: eligible P2P failure → T+1; merchant non-confirmation → T+5; ₹100 per overdue day. | “Miss RBI’s reversal deadline, and eligible cases incur one hundred rupees per overdue day.” |
| **14–20s** | Show the 22-case starting ledger. Click **Run agents · next 3**. Highlight the first selected case. | “Start with the exception ledger. One click processes three cases, one at a time.” |
| **20–29s** | Show the master handing off to Investigator. Zoom into actual source calls and the failure marker on the payment chain. | “The master coordinates the investigation. The Investigator checks bank and network records to locate the failure.” |
| **29–37s** | Follow the RBI Policy agent, then its governance record. Highlight the deadline, compensation and passed/held status. | “The Policy agent checks RBI deadlines and compensation. A mandatory governance gate controls whether financial action can proceed.” |
| **37–45s** | Show Resolver’s proposal followed by executed actions and actual receipt references. | “The Resolver proposes the remedy. The execution engine rechecks the evidence before posting a refund or returning funds.” |
| **45–52s** | Clearly labelled cut: “Another case · Human approval.” Open T21 or T22 and show the held amount and proposed actions. | “Higher-value payouts wait for approval. Conflicting records go to investigation, without speculative refunds.” |
| **52–64s** | Four genuine sponsor shots, about three seconds each: neatlogs trace, Entire checkpoint, cfo.ai model, Crustdata research. Label each role. | “neatlogs makes agent work observable. Entire records the build. cfo.ai models the business. Crustdata supports target-bank research.” |
| **64–70s** | Return to a completed case. Show its real elapsed time, receipt and evidence. Overlay: “Under 60 seconds: our target.” | “Resolution recorded. Evidence attached. Our next milestone: resolving eligible exceptions in under sixty seconds.” |
| **70–75s** | Clean end card: DisputePro, “Built at neatHack,” actual public URL and “Built by Prabhat · prabhatgp.me.” | “DisputePro. Faster recovery, with governance built in. Try the bank desk.” |

Recording and editing requirements:

- Record a complete real run first. Compress waiting periods in the edit, with a visible **“Time-compressed recording”** label. Preserve the actual elapsed timer.
- Never make a 65-second run appear to have completed in 20 seconds. Under 60 seconds is a target, not a verified guarantee.
- Use the measured time from the footage being shown. Do not attach an old model’s timing to a new deployment-model run.
- Keep **“Sandbox demonstration”** visible but unobtrusive.
- Show model labels, meaningful tool results and the governance decision so viewers understand that agents are doing the work.
- Distinguish **proposed** actions from **executed** actions. The approval cut is a separate case, not the next stage of the completed refund.
- Entire, cfo.ai and Crustdata are build/business tools, not sources of payment evidence.
- Do not include an unsupported 1% industry failure claim or the incorrect “80 million failures” number.
- Do not reset the ledger or restart services while a case is working.
- If footage is unavailable, identify what must be recorded; never fabricate successful execution or sponsor activity.
- Add captions with short phrases, not paragraphs. Keep source references and important UI values readable.
- Deliver the final MP4, subtitle file, thumbnail and editable video project.

---

**My recommendation: one EC2 instance, one HTTPS URL, and this 75-second evidence-led demo.** No AWS resources have been created in this turn.
